A short, intuition-first tour of the ocean physics that powers the
capstone — written for people fluent in PDEs and ML but not in
oceanography. The goal is to read the equations in [Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd)
not as a list of symbols but as a familiar set of mechanisms in a
new domain: temperature transported by flow, smeared by turbulence,
heated by sunlight, exchanged with the atmosphere at one boundary
and with the deep ocean at the other.

## 8.1 Why oceans? Why PDEs?

Oceans store and move heat at a rate that dominates the planet's
climate. A back-of-the-envelope: the top 100 m of the ocean has
roughly four times the heat capacity of the entire atmosphere above
it. When the ocean exchanges heat with the air, *the air moves
fast*. So the slow story of ocean heat transport sets the boundary
condition for the fast story of weather — and getting it wrong
matters.

We model that transport with PDEs because the physical processes
involved — advection by currents, diffusion by turbulence, surface
fluxes, radiative absorption — are local and continuous. PDEs are
the natural language for *something at each point in space changes
in response to its neighbours and to external forcings*. The same
mathematics describes heat in a metal rod, pollutant in a river,
neutron flux in a reactor; switching to seawater is mostly a matter
of choosing which terms to keep and which to drop.

This unit is about which terms ocean modellers keep, and *why*.

## 8.2 The column idealisation

Real oceans are three-dimensional, full of eddies, fronts, and
gyres. Modelling that in full takes a supercomputer. But many
questions only require one slice:

> What does temperature look like, as a function of depth, at a
> *single horizontal location*, over a few weeks?

That's the **column idealisation**. We treat the ocean as a stack
of horizontal sheets at fixed $(x, y)$, with $T = T(z, t)$ and
nothing depending on $(x, y)$ inside the column. Horizontal currents
still exist — we don't pretend the ocean is at rest — but their
*effect on the column* is summarised through one quantity: the
vertical velocity $w(z, t)$ those horizontal flows induce via
continuity.

::: {.callout-note}
## When the column idealisation breaks

If you care about ocean fronts (sharp horizontal temperature
gradients), eddies (rotating coherent structures), or coastlines
(boundary effects), the column idealisation fails because the
horizontal physics matters. The capstone problem — a mooring far
from a coastline, far from a front — is exactly the regime where it
works.
:::

The win is dimensionality: a 1D PDE in $(z, t)$ instead of a 3D
system in $(x, y, z, t)$. The cost is that you have to *prescribe*
or *derive* the vertical velocity rather than solve for it; the
horizontal flow that drives it lives in a separate, lower-cost 2D
model (the shallow water solver in [Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd)).

## 8.3 Advection and diffusion in fluids

Two transport mechanisms move heat around the column.

### Advection — temperature riding along with a moving fluid

If a parcel of water is rising at speed $w > 0$, it carries its
temperature with it. A *fixed sensor* at depth $z$ then sees the
temperature of the parcel that *used to be* at depth $z - w \Delta t$.
That's advection:

$$\left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}\right|_{\text{advection}}
= -w\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial z}.$$

The minus sign is the same minus sign you see in the linear
advection equation $u_t + cu_x = 0$ from [Unit 6](../unit_06/unit_06.qmd):
rightward motion at fixed location feels like the field shifted
leftward in space.

In ocean terms: upwelling ($w > 0$) brings cold deep water up past
your sensor; downwelling ($w < 0$) brings warm surface water down.
Either way, *the parcel doesn't change temperature on the way* —
advection just relocates it.

### Diffusion — turbulent stirring as a Fickian closure

Real ocean turbulence is chaotic on scales below ~1 m. We don't
resolve it. What we *do* notice is that, averaged over a few
minutes, turbulence mixes the column the way molecular diffusion
mixes a gas — gradient-down, with an effective diffusivity $\kappa$
many orders of magnitude larger than the molecular value:

$$\left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}\right|_{\text{diffusion}}
= \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\!\left(\kappa(z, t)\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial z}\right).$$

This is the **Reynolds closure** applied to temperature: we replace
unresolved fluctuations by an effective transport coefficient. The
coefficient is large near the wind-driven surface (the *mixed
layer*) and small at depth.

The two mechanisms compete. The **Péclet number** $\mathrm{Pe} = wH /
\kappa$ measures who wins on the column scale: $\mathrm{Pe} \gg 1$ is
advection-dominated, $\mathrm{Pe} \ll 1$ is diffusion-dominated, and
$\mathrm{Pe} \sim 1$ is the messy interesting case the AIMS column
lives in (see §8.6).

## 8.4 Surface energy budget

Heat enters and leaves the ocean through the air-sea interface.
Modelling that exchange properly is an entire field. For our
purposes the budget splits into two parts:

**Penetrating shortwave $Q_{\text{SW}}$.** Sunlight passes *through*
the surface and is absorbed *inside* the water, exponentially with
depth — red light absorbed in the top few centimetres, blue–green
light reaching tens of metres. This is a **body source**, not a
boundary flux.

**Non-penetrating fluxes $Q_{\text{np}}$.** Longwave radiation,
sensible heat, latent heat (evaporation). All act *at* the surface
and add up to a single boundary flux. Cooling typically wins at
night and on cloudy days; heating wins on still sunny afternoons.

The boundary condition at $z = 0$ becomes a Neumann condition on
the diffusive flux of temperature, sourced by $Q_{\text{np}}$. The
penetrating shortwave shows up as a body source $\mathcal{S}(z, t)$
in the equation interior. The full forms are in
[Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) §9.4 and §9.5.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A useful intuition

The ocean is a *heat capacitor* whose plates are the air–sea
interface (top) and a deep reservoir (bottom). The capacitor charges
when net surface flux is positive and discharges to the deep when it
isn't. Diurnal forcing wiggles the charge state on a 24-hour
timescale; storm events kick it on a 1–3 day timescale; seasonal
forcing shifts it over months. *Each regime lives at a different
depth* because the diffusive penetration depth scales as
$\sqrt{\kappa\, \tau}$.
:::

## 8.5 Stratification, mixing, and the deep boundary

Ocean temperature usually decreases with depth — warm sun-heated
water on top, cold deep water below, with a sharp transition called
the **thermocline** in between. This is **stable stratification**:
buoyancy resists mixing because warm parcels want to rise.

The eddy diffusivity $\kappa$ therefore isn't constant. In the
mixed layer (above the thermocline, vigorously stirred by wind and
breaking surface waves), $\kappa$ is large — $\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})$ m²/s.
Below the thermocline, stratification suppresses mixing and $\kappa$
collapses to a background $\mathcal{O}(10^{-5})$ m²/s. The transition
between the two is parametrised by a **Richardson number**
$\mathrm{Ri} = N^2 / (\partial_z U)^2$ comparing buoyancy frequency
$N$ to shear $\partial_z U$ — stable when $\mathrm{Ri} > 1/4$.

At the *bottom* of the column we need another boundary condition.
We pick a simple one — a **fixed deep reservoir** $T(-H, t) = T_{\text{deep}}$
— and treat it as exact. Physically: below the modelled column lies
a much larger volume of cold deep water whose temperature responds
on timescales irrelevant to ours. Dirichlet is a fair model;
zero-flux (an insulating floor) is an alternative if the deep ocean
beneath you is essentially a wall.

## 8.6 Dimensionless regimes

A few dimensionless groups carry most of the physics. They tell you
*which* terms dominate in a given problem before you solve anything.

| Group | Definition | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Péclet $\mathrm{Pe}$ | $wH/\kappa$ | advection vs. diffusion across the column |
| Diffusive time $T_\kappa$ | $H^2/\kappa$ | time for diffusion to mix the column |
| Richardson $\mathrm{Ri}$ | $N^2/(\partial_z U)^2$ | stability of stratification against mixing |
| Diurnal-to-diffusive | $\tau_d / T_\kappa$ | how localised the daily cycle stays in depth |
| Storm-to-diffusive | $\tau_{\text{storm}} / T_\kappa$ | how deep a storm signal penetrates |

For the AIMS column with $H = 100$ m, $\kappa_m = 10^{-3}$ m²/s,
$w_0 = 10^{-5}$ m/s:

- $\mathrm{Pe} \approx 1$ — balanced regime; both transport
  mechanisms compete on equal footing.
- $T_\kappa \approx 116$ days — a 30-day run only mixes a *fraction*
  of the column.
- $\tau_d / T_\kappa \sim 10^{-2}$ — the diurnal cycle is much
  faster than bulk mixing, so it lives in a thin near-surface
  layer.

These three numbers explain almost every qualitative behaviour
you'll see in the toy tasks in [Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) §9.8:
why the diurnal warm layer is thin, why a 3-day storm leaves a
fingerprint deeper than naive cooling would suggest, why SST cools
slowly under upwelling, and why the steady state is reached only
over many months.

## 8.7 From concepts to the AIMS column

The capstone in [Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) is the column
idealisation written down concretely:

- One PDE: $\partial_t T + w \partial_z T = \partial_z(\kappa
  \partial_z T) + \mathcal{S}$.
- Two boundary conditions: Neumann at the surface, Dirichlet at the
  deep reservoir.
- Four prescribed forcings: $w(z, t)$ (from a 2D shallow-water
  solver), $\kappa(z, t)$ (closure), $Q_{\text{np}}(t)$
  (non-penetrating fluxes), $Q_{\text{SW}}(t)$ (penetrating
  shortwave, sourced via Beer–Lambert).
- A reference parameter set tuned for a tropical-reef site.

Everything else — the toy tasks, the storm scenario, the inverse
problem — is choosing which parts of that setup to perturb. The
"science" sits in §§8.2–8.6 above; the implementation sits in
[Unit 10](../unit_10/unit_10.qmd).
